Cleaning a fish tank doesn't always mean draining it. In this method, waste and debris are removed while the water stays in place. Tools like siphon vacuums and filtration systems pull out uneaten food, algae, and sediment from the gravel, keeping the environment clean without stressing the fish. What makes this approach effective is balance. Beneficial bacteria remain undisturbed, water chemistry stays stable, and the tank continues to cycle naturally. It's a low-impact way to maintain a healthy aquarium, showing how smart maintenance can work with the ecosystem instead of resetting it. This video is for educational purposes only. The Aquarium "Waste" You've Been Removing By Mistake! For decades, aquarium keepers have been told that mulm is something that should be removed during routine maintenance. Gravel vacuums, siphons, and deep substrate cleaning have become standard practice throughout the hobby, all with the goal of removing what many people consider to be waste. But what if we've been throwing away one of the most valuable parts of a healthy aquarium ecosystem? In this video, I take a deep dive into the science behind mulm, exploring what it is, how it forms, and why a growing body of research suggests it may play an important role in nutrient recycling, biological filtration, food webs, and long-term aquarium stability. We begin by looking at the difference between detritus and mulm. Although the terms are often used interchangeably, they are not the same thing. Detritus consists of relatively fresh organic matter such as fish waste, uneaten food, and decaying plant material. Mulm is what that detritus becomes after it has been partially broken down by bacteria, fungi, protozoa, worms, and countless other microorganisms. The result is the fine brown material commonly found around plants, hardscape, and substrate surfaces in mature aquariums. From there, we explore one of the most overlooked aspects of modern aquarium science: the role of heterotrophic bacteria. Research has shown that some heterotrophic bacteria can rapidly remove ammonium through a process known as ammonia assimilation, converting it into additional bacterial biomass. Because heterotrophic bacteria often reproduce much faster than traditional nitrifying bacteria, they may provide an important buffer against ammonia spikes in our aquariums. We also look at heterotrophic nitrification and aerobic denitrification, where certain bacterial strains have been shown to process ammonium into nitrite, nitrate, and even nitrogen gas. These pathways offer a fascinating alternative to the traditional ammonia → nitrite → nitrate model that most aquarists are taught when learning about the nitrogen cycle. The video also covers nitrifying microorganisms and the important role mulm can play as a colonisation surface. Research has confirmed that nitrifying bacteria, ammonia-oxidising archaea, and other nitrogen-processing microorganisms can colonise sediment-like environments, helping to support the biological filtration capacity of an aquarium. Rather than choosing between heterotrophic bacteria and nitrifying bacteria, ecosystem aquariums benefit from encouraging both groups and taking advantage of multiple nitrogen-processing pathways simultaneously. Moving beyond filtration, we then explore nutrient recycling. One of the biggest benefits of mulm is its ability to act like a slow-release fertiliser. As microorganisms continuously break down organic matter, nutrients are mineralised and released back into the water column where they can be used by aquatic plants. This is one of the reasons many heavily planted aquariums can thrive with little or no additional fertilisation beyond fish food. I also discuss my own "fish poop fertilisation" approach, where fish waste, uneaten food, and decaying plant matter are recycled naturally by the aquarium ecosystem. In low-tech planted tanks, this nutrient recycling process can significantly reduce or even eliminate the need for liquid fertilisers and root tabs while still supporting healthy plant growth. #aquarium  #fishtank  #fishkeeping  #tropicalfish  #walstad  #walstadmethod
